description_full: Marathon Petroleum Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, operates as an integrated downstream energy company in the United States. The company operates through three segments: Refining & Marketing; Midstream; and Renewable Diesel. The Refining & Marketing segment refines crude oil and other feedstocks at its refineries in the Gulf Coast, Mid-Continent, and West Coast regions of the United States; and purchases refined products and ethanol for resale and distributes refined products through transportation, storage, distribution, and marketing services. Its refined products include transportation fuels, such as reformulated gasolines and blend-grade gasolines; heavy fuel oil; and asphalt. This segment also manufactures propane and petrochemicals. The company sells refined products to wholesale marketing customers in the United States and internationally, buyers on the spot market, and independent entrepreneurs who operate primarily Marathon branded outlets, as well as through long-term fuel supply contracts to direct dealer locations primarily under the ARCO brand. The Midstream segment gathers, transports, stores, distributes, and markets crude oil and refined products, including renewable diesel and other hydrocarbon-based products through refining logistics assets, pipelines, terminals, towboats, and barges; gathers, processes, and transports natural gas; and transports, fractionates, stores, and markets natural gas liquids. The Renewable Diesel segment processes renewable feedstocks into renewable diesel, markets, and distributes renewable diesel through its Midstream segment and third parties. It sells renewable diesel to wholesale marketing customers, buyers on the spot market, and through long-term supply contracts to direct dealers under the ARCO brand. Marathon Petroleum Corporation was founded in 1887 and is headquartered in Findlay, Ohio.

financial_summary: Marathon Petroleum Corporation is a large-cap energy business with a $112.9B market cap on $132.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -9% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 16% against a 8% cost of capital, a 8-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $4.8B in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.04× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.5× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.5×.

Shareholder yield of 4.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Operating margins 9% below sector median — a cost disadvantage the moat cannot hide
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Priced near or above estimated fair value, so the margin of safety has been bid away
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $12.8M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
The commodity cycle — revenue and free cash flow are ultimately hostage to a price the company does not set, and the long-run energy-transition arc adds a structural overhang.
ESG-driven capital flight and stranded asset risk — tightening climate policy and investor mandates raise the cost of capital and risk leaving reserves permanently in the ground.
Geopolitical supply shocks — wars, sanctions, and OPEC decisions create volatility that no hedging programme can fully neutralise.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 149% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 16% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 38% and a beta of 0.70, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.54 vs 5y 0.56), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $915.3M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 73% in the 2020 crash and 30% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $405 (margin of safety -2%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 28%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $286 to $574 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Energy peers: cheaper on P/E 8.2 vs 13.6, richer on P/FCF 23.7 vs 14.6 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 282% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 17 covering analysts target $462 on average, 11% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 16% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 8pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.83).
It converts 4% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.04x.
ROE of 23% is amplified by 4.8x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.1% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.5x net debt to EBITDA ($3.7B of cash against $32.9B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.5x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -9.2% over 3 years, 13.7% over 5 years and 6.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 30%).
At current returns, reinvesting 25% of profits supports about 3.9% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 2.6% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 17, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 50.4% on average.
Analysts expect -10.8% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 80%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (16 sales, net $12.8M sold).
It returns 4.1% a year to shareholders (3.1% in buybacks and 1.1% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 14.0% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 14 consecutive years, though it has been cut 5.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 18,500 employees, each generates about $7.2M of revenue, 3.5x the Energy median, and revenue has grown 3.8% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $258K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.2M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
